match.reason: No bank point teaches the contact versus non-contact distinction; the closest cards define forces and gravity but do not classify friction, magnetic and electrostatic forces by whether they need touching.

draft.title: Contact and non-contact forces
card: A force is a push or a pull on an object. It is measured in newtons (N).
a force that needs the two objects to touch. Friction is one: it acts where two surfaces rub or try to slide past each other.
a force that acts across a gap, with no touching. Gravity, magnetic forces and electrostatic forces are all non-contact forces.
A magnet can pull a paper clip across a gap. A balloon rubbed on hair can pick up small bits of paper without touching them. Both are forces at a distance.
draft.remember: Contact forces need touching. Non-contact forces act across a gap.

a.q: Which of these is a contact force?
opts: Friction between a shoe and the floor
Gravity pulling an apple off a tree
A magnet pulling a nail towards it
A charged comb lifting tiny paper pieces
a.why: Friction acts where two surfaces touch, so it is a contact force. Gravity, magnetic and electrostatic forces all act across a gap.
a.clue: Which force needs two surfaces to be touching?

b.q: Leila rubs a plastic ruler on her jumper. It then lifts small bits of paper from her desk without touching them. What kind of force lifts the paper?
opts: A non-contact force, because it acts across a gap
A contact force, because the ruler pushes the paper
A contact force, because Leila rubbed the ruler
A non-contact force, because it is a type of friction
b.why: The ruler does not touch the paper, so the force acts at a distance. That makes it a non-contact (electrostatic) force. The rubbing is only how the ruler was charged.
b.clue: Does the ruler touch the paper when it lifts it?

a.best: Friction between a shoe and the floor

b.best: A non-contact force, because it acts across a gap
